title: Platform seller story arc — quick trust lab (draft)
slide_headings: 1 — 30s hook: why latency and cost kill rollouts
4 — Economics: predictable unit costs and caching wins
content:
Purpose: Give platform-facing sellers a compact, repeatable story that emphasizes reliability-first inference economics and a low-friction pilot ask. This is intentionally terse — build as a 6-slide deck for 8–12 minute customer conversations.

Narrative thread (speaker notes):
- Opening hook (30s): start with a tight pain line: "You built a great product feature — then production inference costs or jitter killed adoption." Pause for cue. Frame Redwood as the runtime that decouples model selection from serving economics.
- Evidence (90s): 2 microcases: (1) fintech chat summarization: reduced median tail latency from 780ms to 140ms after prefix caching + KV locality; (2) marketplace search reranker: 3.2x throughput uplift with adaptive batching and 18% lower per-token bill after quantization profile. Use simple metrics only — latency P95, cost per 1k requests, time to onboard model.
- Engineering safety (90s): explain staged fallbacks: model variant routing (high-precision -> mid-tier quantized) + region fallback + graceful degradation to short-answer templates. Emphasize that fallbacks are policy-driven and testable with canaries. Call out observability hooks (token-level cost traces, per-route SLOs) that make incident triage easy.
- Economics (60s): show a single slide with three levers: caching (prefix/KV), microbatching, and quantization. Give example numbers: caching can cut token volume by ~20–40% for multi-turn chat; batching improves utilization for bursty workloads resulting in 1.5–2x effective throughput; quant profiles trade 2–4% absolute quality loss for 30–60% GPU cost reductions depending on model. Provide a simple ROI line: pilot with 100k monthly requests should see measurable cost per feature drop within two weeks.
- Pilot ask (30s): request a 2–4 week pilot: ingest 2–3 representative prompts, run A/B (baseline vs Redwood routing/config), define one success metric (p95 latency < target OR 20% drop in per-feature cost) and one safety gate (no >5% accuracy loss on eval set). Offer Redwood’s pilot template and a two-hour engineering kickoff.

Appendix materials (quick reference for seller):
- Roleplay prompts: "Customer: we can’t risk hallucinations — how do you prevent it?" -> Response: fallbacks + eval prompt set + per-rollout regression alerts + canary rollback policy.
- Rapid rebuttals: 
  * "Your pricing is unpredictable" -> show reserved capacity + dedicated plan pricing and per-token transparency in console.
  * "We can self-host cheaper" -> acknowledge but highlight engineering cost to reach same SLOs, ops burden, and auditability. Offer comparative checklist.
- Pre-call checklist (one-pager): customer workload type, expected QPS and burst profile, acceptable p95 latency, primary quality metric, security/regulatory constraints, data residency requirement, stakeholders (platform eng, security, product).

Design notes and constraints: keep slides light on words; prefer one chart per slide. Use a single customer microcase visual (timeline: onboarding -> canary -> steady-state gains). Keep technical appendix in 2–3 extra slides for SEs.

Open questions to resolve before next iteration:
- Get precise quantization delta for common open models (Llama 2 13B) from infra research team.
- Obtain a short quote from a pilot customer for the evidence slide.
- Add a small diagram showing runtime routing policy (latency->region->variant) — ask infra for a simple SVG.

Immediate next steps (owner: Morgan):
1) Groom slide content into a draft deck (this week).
2) Sync with Ethan for numbers (Monday).
3) Run roleplay with Sofia and Priya and capture top 5 objections to add to appendix (Tue).

Notes-to-self: rough timings work for 8–12 minute delivery. We should produce two variants: (A) platform-architect focused with deeper SLO/econ slides, (B) buyer-friendly with more outcome stories and financial anchors.

End of draft.
speaker_notes: Keep the opening to 30s, avoid model names unless asked, use outcomes and numbers. For technical SE follow-up: bring simple canary checklist and sample eval prompts. If security asks about data handling, point them to the Private deployment docs and note KMS/HSM options.
quick_rebuttals: Pricing unpredictability -> reserved capacity and per-token transparency + console cost breakdown
Self-host cheaper -> upfront engineering + SLO maintenance + hidden ops costs = often higher long term
Model quality tradeoffs -> controlled quant profiles, per-prompt evals, and canary rollouts ensure regressions are caught
